Third, pushing forward financing for development and development cooperation. We reaffirmed the importance of development cooperation through continued international cooperation and official development assistance. Fourth, to continue the fight against poverty and hunger. In conclusion, Mr. Vice Chair, the United Nations at 80 has not solved the world's problems, but it remains one of the best places to tackle them and develop multilateral solutions and partnerships in financing climate action, promoting innovation, inclusion, and resilience for the sustainable development of our peoples and our planet. The Philippines stands ready to work with all delegations at this session of the Second Committee in this spirit towards these ends for our United Nations. Thank you.

Since November 2023, there has been no sign of life from Biping, and there is a serious concern for his life. As Israel eagerly awaits the return of our sons and daughter, and for the burial of our dead, we also wait for the return of Joshua, so his family will be able to bring his body home in dignity, and for the return of Biping, so hopefully, and I do pray that this will be the case, He will be able to reunite with his family. 48 innocent hostages remain captive in Gaza. If everything goes as planned, when we'll meet here again on Monday, we will see them back home. Colleagues, the next few days are critical and will be especially sensitive. Israel has already taken steps to bring the war to an end. Many member states in our region and worldwide have shown support and reflect broad coalition for peace. Thank you Mr. chair distinguished delegates ladies and gentlemen it is a privilege to take the floor on behalf of my country in the session of the second committee Let me begin by expressing our full support for the work of this Committee, which remains essential in shaping the economic and financial agenda of the UN and in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals. My country aligns with the statement delivered earlier by the EU, and in addition, we would like to make the following remarks in our national capacity. From climate shocks and geopolitical rivalry to deepening inequalities, economic fragmentation, and mounting debt burdens, we are witnessing challenges that transcend borders and require a shared response. Financing for development must unite strategy, capital, and multilateral support in a coherent ecosystem, which is why the fourth UN Conference on Financing for Development and its outcome document held in Seville this past July was timely and of utmost importance. Being a responsible party of the global contract, We supported the Seville commitment on financing for development, and we will continue to work on increasing financing for sustainable development in the country and ensuring that no one is left behind. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The outside, I'd like to extend my sincere congratulations to Ambassador Dliba on his election as the chair of the second committee and to the members of the Bureau. You may count on Albania's full support and active engagement in ensuring a constructive and forward-looking session. As we convene for the 80th session of the General Assembly, the world found itself at a defining juncture. Conflicts, poverty, inequalities, and the intensifying impacts of climate change continue to test the resilience of our societies. the same time, new technologies, growing interdependence, and global solidarity offer unprecedented opportunities for progress. In this complex global landscape, multilateral cooperation remains indispensable. Albania firmly believes that the United Nations, and particularly this committee, must stand at the heart of our collective response, translating shared commitments into concrete results that improve the lives of people everywhere. With less than five years remaining to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, the time for accelerated action is now. Mr. Chair, Albania aligns itself with the statement delivered earlier by the European Union and its member states. Allow me to highlight several points of particular importance from a national perspective. First, we must intensify implementation of the 2030 agenda. The Pact for the Future provides a renewed political framework for advancing the SDGs, but our success will be measured not by new declarations, but by tangible progress on the ground. Albania continues to integrate the SDGs across our national strategy for development and European integration, promoting sustainable growth, quality education, social inclusion, and gender equality as cross-cutting priorities. We are committed to ensuring that our national development policies contribute to the global effort to eradicate poverty in all its forms, reduce inequalities, and promote decent work and opportunities for all. Second, addressing the triple planetary crisis, climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution must remain at the core of our deliberations. Albania, situated in one of the most climate-vulnerable regions of Europe, is already witnessing the effects of environmental degradation. We are working to accelerate our green transition to renewable energy, improved waste management, and sustainable use of natural resources. We continue to support ambitious international action under the Paris Agreement and look forward to meaningful progress at COP30 in Belm. We also encourage deeper cooperation between regions and stronger international support for adaptation resilience, particularly for countries and communities most affected by climate impacts. Albania has made notable progress in digital governments, with nearly all public services now accessible online, enhancing transparency and efficiency. Yet the global digital divide persists. The implementation of the Global Digital Compact offers an opportunity to ensure that digital technologies are inclusive, secure, and human-centered, while the upcoming WSIS+20 review should help guide a more coherent international approach. Fourth, the eradication of poverty and the promotion of social injustice must remain at the heart of our work. The forthcoming World Social Summit will be a critical moment to renew our global social contract, anchored in decent work, universal social protection, and equality for all. Albania strongly supports this process and will continue to champion policies that empower youth and women, expand access to education, and ensure that no one is left behind. Let us seize this milestone session to reaffirm our shared commitment to solidarity, partnership, and the promise of sustainable development for all, leaving no one behind. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Somalia, and I now give the floor to the distinguished Permanent Representative of Samoa. Excellency, you have the floor.

But too often, we simply rebrand and recycle old ideas while failing to deliver tangible results. Meanwhile, multilateralism is under threat and international financial commitment are being eroded. Overseas development assistance is a clear example. Today, the financing gap for achieving the SDG exceeds $4 trillion. Yet, when it comes to funding wars, resources are never in short supply. The stark contrast should give us all pause. We must confront the deep inequities embedded in the global economic and financial architecture. Yesterday's solutions are no match for today's crisis. A modern, just, and inclusive financial system must be created, one that recognizes us, understands us, and that works for us. We therefore look forward to the timely implementation of the severe commitment. It must be scaled up, easily accessible, devoid of burdensome conditions, and tailored to the needs of small island developing states. As climate related shock intensify, we stress the importance of prearranged finance and early action solution. Instruments such as the Risk-Informed Early Action Partnership and the MVI must be swiftly adopted by IFIs, MDPs and development partners to ensure timely and targeted resource allocation. We welcome The Secretary-General's UN80 initiative reform must translate to real impact on the ground, especially for SIDS, by eliminating duplication, enhancing coherence, and accelerating delivery. Mr. President, Madam President, Samoa remains steadfast in our commitment to the sustainable stewardship of our ocean. It is time to fundamentally transform our relationship with the ocean from a resource we exploit to one we protect and cherish. Without urgent action, states face a future without land and no usable ocean. Gender equality must remain a cross-cutting priority in all our development and cooperation effort at home Samoa has made strong progress through legislative reform, institutional mechanism, increased women's leadership participation, and expanded access to health and education for women and girls. Non-communicable diseases are now the leading health challenge in my country. We welcome the high-level meeting on NCDs and call for specific targeted action for six, particularly in prevention, health food system and sustainable financing. Energy is both a driver and accelerator for some more sustainable development ambition. Digital transformation, including AI and data-driven planning, offer tools to accelerate an inclusive just energy transition, especially through off-grid solutions. And while we acknowledge the transformative potential of STI, including artificial intelligence in advancing sustainable development, we urge caution regarding their associated risk. Mr. President, for SIDS, resilience is not an option. It is a matter of survival. Inclusivity must be the foundation of global economic reform. The rule of the global economy cannot be written without those most affected. Whether designing liquidity instrument or debt relief framework, we must be co-creators, not bystanders. This is not just about fairness. It is about building a system that lasts. Exclusion weakens us all. A global economy cannot be sustainable, inclusive, or resilient unless it is also fair, adaptive, and climate-aligned. Thank you very much.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Samoa, and now I'll give the floor to the Permanent Observer of the Holy See.

Thank you, thank you, Madam Chair. My delegation would like to extend its congratulations to you, to the Chair, and the members of the Bureau on your election, and to assure you of its constructive engagement and full support throughout the work of this session. The context in which States adopted the 2030 Agenda has undergone significant change. The pursuit of sustainable development has been hindered by a number of factors, including armed conflicts, climate change, economic fragility, and the pandemic. In this regard, my delegation reaffirms that sustainable development can only be considered authentic when it advances integral development, that is, the development of every person and the whole person. Consequently, development cannot be comprehended exclusively in economic terms. It must also foster the cultural and spiritual development of all people, Integral development is therefore the overarching metric against which the collective efforts of the international community should be measured. This vision accepts the imperative of eradicating poverty in all its forms and dimension, a task recognized as the greatest global challenge and the indispensable requirement for sustainable development. Furthermore, There is a moral imperative for the eradication of poverty. Poverty in its various forms represent a significant infringement on the God-given dignity of every human being, impeding the potential of individual and the exclusion from full participation in community life. Therefore, poverty eradication cannot be an afterthought in development. It must remain its central and primary priority. Madam Chair, the Second Committee plays a vital role in ensuring that this central priority remains at the heart of the multilateral agenda. Indeed, the Committee's work is inextricably linked to people, their needs and aspirations, and about the choices made by the international community, either fostering hope or allowing despair to take root. For this reason, my delegation urges that poverty eradication remain the touchstone for all discussions in this forum. All too often, other issues, however important, have diverted attention away from this fundamental objective. In the final five years to 2030, it is crucial that poverty eradication lie at the very heart of everything this Committee strives to achieve. Madam Chair, Prior to the exploration of multilateral solutions for sustainable development, it is imperative to reaffirm that multilateralism represents the sole viable avenue for progress. With these considerations in mind and in this final five-year push, it is essential that multilateralism be grounded in a revitalized spirit of human fraternity. This spirit is not merely a sentimental ideal, but rather a practical necessity. Pope Leo has encouraged the international community to continue to nurture the spirituality of fraternity through culture, working relationship, and diplomatic action. Adopting this perspective has the potential to transform our approach to global challenges, moving us from a logic of indifference and isolation to one of shared responsibility and cooperative action. The United Nations continue to serve as a beacon of hope for multilateralism. In a world increasingly fractured by conflict and division, these institutions represent the conviction that dialogue and cooperation are the only lasting route to peace and development. Indeed, the attainment of this common good has become a goal that is beyond the reach of individual states. Such an understanding for a broader vision of solidarity in the pursuit of integral development transcends the limitation of short-term national interests. Madam Chair, the vision of multilateralism for the common good is at odds with the current context of rising military expenditure and falling official development assistance commitments. While military budgets surge to $2.7 trillion in 2024, the annual financing gap for the sustainable development goals is estimated to be $4 trillion. Every increase in military spending represents resources that could have been used to meet people's basic needs and to establish a lasting peace. Rather than being invested in health care, education, and food systems, these resources are being diverted toward weapons that destroy lives and livelihoods. As Pablo has lamented, money that could be used to build new hospitals and schools is instead being used to destroy those that already exist. This paradox undermines the spirit of fraternity on which multilateralism depends, making the goal of sustainable development increasingly unattainable. Madam Chair, in the final five years leading up to 2030, it is evident that a renewed commitment to multilateralism provides the most reliable basis for lasting solutions. By embracing multilateralism rooted in solidarity, the international community can still protect human dignity, foster hope, and achieve integral development for all. Thank you.
I thank the Permanent Observer of the Holy See for the statement. And now I give the floor to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of the OECD. And now I'll give the floor to the representative of the Pan-African Intergovernmental Agency for Water and Sanitation for Africa.

We welcome deeper engagement with UN agencies and look forward to continued contribution to the Committee's deliberations. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Pan-African Intergovernmental Agency for Water and Sanitation for Africa. And now I give the floor to the representative of the International Telecommunication Union.

Thank you, Madam Chair. The International Telecommunication Union has been a driving force in fostering multi-stakeholder action to create an equitable information society. And we have three reasons to acknowledge that commitment this year. It's the 160th anniversary of the ITU and 40 years since ITU identified the digital divide and began to bridge it. And this December, the General Assembly will convene a high-level meeting to review the outcomes from the first World Summit of the Information Society held 20 years ago. That summit, convened by ITU, was the first to emphasize multi-stakeholder engagement and to include the private sector as a partner. This approach has become a fundamental principle for our work, and we are pleased to see that it's recognized in the draft outcome document for WSIS+20. That draft does make reference to the private sector 17 times. But most of those references are in the general call for multi-stakeholder engagement, with little attention given to its specific contribution to digital innovation. 2.6 billion people are still excluded from our digital world, and it will take $2.8 trillion in infrastructure to connect them. This isn't going to be possible without significant investment by the private sector. However, the private sector is notably absent from key sections in the WSIS zero draft, where its involvement is critical, including the digital economy, social and economic development, the enabling environment, and capacity building. And it overlooks the role of the private sector in fostering a digital environment that supports micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises through tools like e-commerce and digital payments. Also, some references to the public sector, like those found in the data governance section of that zero draft, do not fully capture the extent of its role. For example, the private sector is recognized as a contributor of data without recognizing its role in generating, managing, and innovating data systems. Similarly, in the human rights section, there is an emphasis on mitigating potential harms caused by information and communication technologies, but the enabling role ICTs play in advancing rights and access to health, education and expression is not acknowledged. ITU, the specialized UN agency for digital technologies, has more than 1,000 private sector members, and we view WSIS as a chance to reinforce and strengthen collaboration with them and all of our stakeholders. With five years to go till 2030, it's critical to mobilize private sector support for sustainable and inclusive development. We're dedicated to making sure the WSIS Action Lines achieve real results in partnership with the private sector, civil society, and our member states. And we urge the second committee to recognize this, recognize this, and to support policies that harness multi-stakeholder expertise and this private sector spirit of innovation to achieve universal and affordable digital connectivity for all. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of the ITU for the statement. And now I give the floor to the Regional Commissions New York Office.

Madam Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the five United Nations regional commissions. Allow me to start by congratulating Ambassador Lamin Dibba of the Gambia on his election as chair of the Second Committee, as well as the members of the Bureau. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the theme of the general debate resonates strongly with the critical task ahead of us. to accelerate progress on the 2030 agenda through renewed multilateralism that delivers at scale and speed, grounded in regional cooperation and solidarity. With the clock to 2030 rapidly ticking down, we are reminded that the time for pledges has passed. What is needed now is decisive shift from commitment to action. The regional commissions remain firmly committed to supporting the Second Committee in advancing inclusive, sustainable, and resilient development. As the regional arm of the United Nations, the regional commissions connect global deliberations and agreements with national realities, helping countries turn the 2030 Agenda into concrete action. The 2025 Regional Forum for Sustainable Development sent a clear message. Progress towards SDGs is too slow, but momentum for transformation is growing. Countries are calling for stronger leadership, deeper regional cooperation, foresight, investment in context-specific solutions, and renewed multilateral solidarity. The regional commissions serve as the regional engines of implementation, linking global ambition with country action through evidence, platform, and partnerships. In this connection, we will intensify efforts in providing the analysis, policy dialogue platforms, and capacity support needed to turn global commitments into regionally tailored solutions. Following the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, we are now helping countries put the severe commitment into practice, including through innovative regional financing mechanisms. Looking ahead, our work focuses on three interconnected priorities. First, scaling up sustainable finance and investment. The regional commissions are helping countries strengthen tax policy, manage debt responsibly, and build more inclusive financial systems. Through regional platforms, we align fiscal tools with climate goals and connect capital providers with sustainable investment opportunities. The recent launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency stands as a clear example of transmo- transformative action through regional partnership. Second, driving structural transformation and inclusion. The Commission support countries in advancing green and digital transitions that generate decent jobs, empower women, and expand opportunities for young people. This includes strengthening regional value chains, promoting the care economy, and investing in innovation and social protection systems that leave no one behind. They are also preparing to help countries translate the upcoming Second World Summit for Social Development in social development commitments into action by building the institutional capacities needed for effective social policies. Third, deepening regional cooperation on shared challenges. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the next five years will define not the fate of 20.
I thank the distinguished representative of the regional commissions, and now I give the floor to the representative of the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

Chair, Excellency, distinguished delegates, thank you for giving me the floor. The Second Committee meet at a time of profound change. Yet momentum for progress remains. From the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development to the Food Systems Summit follow-ups, we have seen renewed political will. The work of this committee plays a crucial role in advancing solution. And we were pleased to hear many delegation underlying the importance of financing for development of agriculture, food security, and nutrition for sustainable development. These are areas, key entry point for investment. As evidence show, in fact, growth in agri-food system is two to three times more effective in reducing poverty, and that every dollar invested in this sector can yield up to $16 in return. In rural areas, home to 80% of the world's poorest people, such targeted investment can fuel growth and stability, and generating over 120 million decent jobs and anchoring thriving local economies. As we approach this important session, IFAD, the International Fund for Agricultural Development, offers three core reflections. First, bold partnership across stakeholders are needed now more than ever to reduce fragmentation and align action. Second, while ODA remains central, resources must be used catalytically through innovative approaches that crowd in financing from all sources, including from the private sector. Third, country-led, people-centered, and market-driven approaches are essential for meaningful results. As a UN specialized agency and international financial institution, IFAD remains fully committed to delivering on the FFD4 outcomes, applying these approaches by acting as a convener, as an enabler of risk, and as an investment platform for rural prosperity to support impact on the ground at speed and at scale. We stand ready to support your deliberation and to turn commitment into action and results on the ground. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of IFAT. And now we therefore conclude the general debate. The committee will now resume its consideration of agenda item 21, countries in special situations, and item 23, operational activities for development, in order to hear the remaining speakers in the joint general discussion. I remind speakers that the time limit is three minutes. We have about eight speakers on the list. So I now give the floor to the first speaker, Cameroon, followed by Bangladesh. Cameroon, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair, for giving me the floor. My delegation wishes to express its firm determination to support LDCs. small island developing states and landlocked developing states. Faced with the systemic challenges that are multiplying, it is urgent that we take concrete action. It should be measurable and adequately financed. In this vein, my country reaffirms its full adherence to the Doha Programme of Action for MICs, to the Abbas and to the Avaza Programme of Action. Our support rests on a strong conviction. We need to support and break our reliance on development assistance, on online universities, and the opportunities for sustainable development are important. Our funders must go beyond 0.2% of GDP and mobilize innovative finance, notably through the DTS reallocated to Africa, SDRs, Special Drawing Rights for Africa. My delegation calls for active solidarity for LDCs through the Antigua and Barbuda Platform for Action and the immediate mobilization of the $100 billion that were promised, a plan of adaptation and access to the Loss and Damage Fund. mechanism. As we recognize the challenges faced by those facing rising sea levels, there are also those who face challenges because of their landlocked status. And we support the Abaza Program of Action, notably supporting continuity of transport and facilitating trade in the transit countries who support regional solidarity. And together with that, Cameroon supports the facilitation, regional integration of youth African exchange. We can no longer rely on words that are empty. We must have additional partnerships and transparency. All of these things are possible if we have firm commitment from all.
I thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of Cameroon. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bangladesh, followed by Qatar. So Bangladesh, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Bangladesh aligns itself with the statements delivered by G77 and China and the LDC group. LDCs and graduating LDCs are on the front lines of multiple interconnected and cascading crises. Rising extreme poverty coincides with diminishing development assistance and decreasing foreign direct investment. The digital divide is also widening. With debt burdens rising, our fiscal space is shrinking, which hinders our ability to invest in health, education, and social protection of our people. In such a scenario, countries in special situations need concessional and grant financing. We need debt solutions that genuinely ease the servicing pressures that we face. Against this backdrop, the Doha Programme of Action must move from promise to action. The Compromises of the Saviya and the OAU Programme of Action adopted this year are right steps forward. But to realize their full potential, we must convert this renewed political will concrete actions. Recovery of stolen assets is of particular importance to us, and we also reiterate our call to extend LDC-specific support measures for graduating countries, with a coordinated and phased withdrawal to make their graduation sustainable and irreversible. Bangladesh is consistently advocating for adequate resource allocation for the offices that serve countries in special situations. It is more so in the context of the UNAT process and associated cost-cutting measures. Madam Chair, Last year, this Committee and the Bureau invested considerable efforts to adopt the landmark QCPR resolution, the final full cycle QCPR before 2030, with consensus. We urge that the implementation of the QCPR remains action-oriented and data-driven, with full ownership and leadership of the programme countries. It is heartening to see that the Secretary-General's 2025 QCPR report shows sustained improvement in coordination, transparent information sharing, and efficient resource use in UN country teams and resident coordinators. However, we are concerned that the resident coordinator system has remained severely underfunded, hindering its ability to support the program countries. Member states, therefore, must prioritize providing the RC system with adequate, predictable, and sustainable financing that it needs. Finally, South-South and triangular cooperation, we reiterate that it should be systematically integrated across UN entity policies, strategic plans and programmes, in line with the Buenos Aires Outcome Document. If meaningfully complemented to the North-South cooperation, it can truly accelerate SDG delivery for countries in special situations. I thank you.
I thank the Distinguished Representative of Bangladesh, and now I'll give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of Qatar.

Said al-Rais.

Moreover, Qatar has welcomed the General Assembly resolution number 78/317, entitled "Antigua and Barbuda Plan of Action for Small Island Developing States," and resolution 79/233, entitled "Program of Work for Landlocked Developing Countries." Ladies and gentlemen, Qatar has always been an active strategic partner in responding to the needs and global challenges and has a rich record in cooperation and partnership. Most of our development assistance, international development assistance, is dedicated to these small developing countries. This was clearly manifested through Qatar's commitment to offer $60 million in financial donations. On the 24th of September 2025, we signed, Qatar signed an agreement with the Office of the High Representative of LDCs, where we will fund two of the outcomes of the Doha program, which is building resilience and a food security program. The General Assembly and Resolution 79/218 has welcomed the offer made by our country to host the high-level comprehensive midpoint review. We'd like to renew our commitment to work with all partners at all levels to support-- microphone has been cut off.

I thank the distinguished representative of the State of Qatar. And now I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia, followed by Gambia and then Tanzania. So Malaysia, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Malaysia aligns itself with the statements delivered by Iraq on behalf of G77 and China, as well as Thailand on behalf of ASEAN. The plight of countries in special situations, including the LDCs, LLDCs continue to demand urgent global attention as they face persistent challenges in achieving sustainable development. This situation underscores the urgency for greater international support and comprehensive reforms to enable these countries to overcome poverty and build resilience in the face of economic and environmental vulnerabilities. Madam Chair, Malaysia views South-South cooperation as a catalyst for the exchange of knowledge, best practices, and resources among developing nations and stakeholders across various issues. In the quest to build back better, Malaysia stands ready to collaborate with other countries, drawing upon our national capabilities, including the Malaysian Technical Cooperation Program, MTCP. The MTCP is a cornerstone of our support for countries in these special situations, focusing on human capital development, technical assistance, and capacity building. Since 1980, over 38,000 participants from 144 countries have benefited from MTCP's training courses. The breadth of these training courses encompasses critical areas such as healthcare, education, agriculture, sustainable development, poverty alleviation, investment promotion, information and communication technologies. Further, Malaysia has also been actively facilitating third country training program, TCTP, under the triangular cooperation framework, working with both global south and north to implement projects that addresses the specific needs of LDCs and LLDCs. It is Malaysia's steadfast belief that intensifying North-South cooperation guided by principles of respect, equality and mutual benefits is crucial in addressing global inequality and inequity. Madam Chair, Malaysia therefore remains resolved in its commitment to South-South cooperation as a key strategy and looks forward to efficient systems in accelerating progress towards the 2030 Agenda, ensuring that no one is left behind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia. And now I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of Gambia.

Thank you, Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. My delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by Iraq on behalf of G77 and China, Nepal on behalf of the LDCs, and wishes to offer a few remarks in our national capacity. The Gambia continues to pursue its national development targets in full alignment with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. As part of this commitment, the country is strengthening implementation of the Doha Programme of Action to Advance Structural Transformation, over to eradication, agricultural development, and climate resilience to accelerate inclusive and economic growth. With support from the government of Turkey, the UN Technology Bank in collaboration with the Ministry of Higher Education, Research, Science, and Technology is implementing initiatives to boost agricultural productivity and advance food security in line with our national development plan and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for the Gambia. Notably, the deployment of post-harvest technologies in cassava value chain has helped reduce post-harvest losses by identifying the most appropriate technologies for improving cassava production, enhance farmers' knowledge, and expand the use of effective post-harvest practices nationwide, with a special focus on empowering women. Furthermore, the partnership is strengthening research and innovation linkages, offering training programs for women and youth cooperatives in cashew producing regions, and facilitating technology transfer and capacity development, all of which have improved productive quality and expanded market access, empowering communities and supporting inclusive growth. The complementary and practical nature of this collaboration makes it an exemplary model for fostering South-South and triangular partnerships, and enabling effective multilateral cooperation to address the special needs of all countries, particularly the most vulnerable. Chair, under our Ministry of Trade, the Gambia is finalizing a national Doha program of action implementation strategy, which aligns with our green recovery focused national development plan to promote private sector growth, industrial diversification, and digital transformation with the aim to increase the incomes and competitiveness of smallholder farmers and SMEs and strengthen national ownership of the DPOA commitments. However, challenges remain, such as low productive capacity, limited access to regional and international markets, minimal structural transformation, high debt burden, and inadequate access to modern technology and climate vulnerability. For these reasons, increased ODA, the capitalization and operationalization of the loss and damage fund, and the continued and sustained support of the OHRLS remains indispensable. We therefore call for strengthening of the office's mandate and resources to enhance its effectiveness and urge member states to fulfill their commitments. The government of the Gambia wishes to express profound appreciation to OHRLS and all partners for their tireless efforts in advocating for and mobilizing the required resources, as well as guiding the implementation of programs that are critical to our sustainable development.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Gambia. And now I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of Tanzania, followed by the Holy See. Tanzania, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam Chair, for the floor. The United Republic of Tanzania aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the Group of 77 and China, and wishes to add the following remarks in its national capacity. We thank the Secretary-General for his comprehensive report on the follow-up to the fifth United Nations Conference on the Least Developed Countries. The report rightly underscore the progress under the Doha Programme of Action remains uneven. While global GDP growth has modestly recovered at 4.1%, least developed countries continue to face high debt burden, climate shocks, limited access to concessional finance. For many, including Tanzania, these persistent constraints call for strengthened international solidarity to sustain resilient socioeconomic gains. Madam Chair, Tanzania appreciates the recognition made by the Committee for Development of Policy regarding the substantial progress achieved towards meeting the graduation threshold. The 2024 triennial review confirms that Tanzania met two of the three criteria, reflecting steady implementation of long and medium-term development plans, strong investments in human capital, and sound macroeconomic management. Infant and maternal mortality have declined, access to education and clean water has expanded, and fiscal and debt framework have improved. Our transition to lower middle income status underscores our commitment to Doha Programme of Action and delivery of Sustainable Development Goals. However, graduation also presents challenges. Our economy remains dependent on agriculture and vulnerable to external and climate-related shocks. Premature withdrawal of LDC-specific support could undermine industrialization, export diversification, and digital transformation. Therefore, Tanzania calls for a smooth, well-supported transition, ensuring continued access to climate finance and dedicated mechanisms such as the IMF's resilience and sustainability facility and the AFDP climate action window. Madam Chair, in conclusion, we urge recognition of Tanzania's special circumstance as a country on the graduation path, but still facing huge multidimensional vulnerability. In this regard, the continued preferential treatment, concession finance, and the capacity building must extend beyond the graduation date to ensure an irreversible and sustainable transmission. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Tanzania, and now I give the floor to the permanent observer of the Holy See.

Thank you, Madam Chair. My delegation welcomes today's debate as an opportunity to recognize and address the unique and persistent vulnerabilities that put countries in special situations at greater risk of lagging behind in the pursuit of sustainable development. At stake are both the achievement of integral development for all and the principle that every country must be treated with equal respect and as an equal partner in the international community, regardless of its size, geographical position, or economic weight. As Pablo reminded us, helping the poor is a matter of justice before a question of philanthropy. Madam Chair, my delegation recognizes that the most pressing and unifying concern for countries in special situation is the unsustainable debt burden. It is widely acknowledged that high debt burdens limit investments in the long-term development and erode the capacity of governments to provide for the most basic needs of their people. And this is true for LDCs, LLDCs, and the SIDS alike. Debt relief, including debt cancellation, is therefore not a marginal issue, but a central prerequisite for achieving sustainable development in these countries. As such, in this jubilee year of the Catholic Church, the Holy See recognizes that debt relief is not only an economic policy choice, but above all, a moral imperative. Madam Chair, the global financial system must be directed towards the goal of attaining the common good of the human family. Therefore, meaningful action on that cannot be separated from the way international institutions are organized. In international agencies, it is necessary that the interests of the whole human family be equally represented. It is necessary, moreover, that in evaluating the consequences of their decisions, these agencies always give sufficient consideration to peoples and countries which have little weight in the international market, but which are burdened by the most acute and desperate needs and are thus more dependent on support for their development. The basic goal is to guide economic processes by ensuring that the God-given dignity of human being and his or her integral development as a person are respected in the context of the common good. Thank you very much.
I thank the Holy See, and now I give the floor to the last speaker on our list for today, which is UN Industrial Development Organization. UNIDO, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to deliver this statement today on behalf of UNIDO. The landmark outcomes of all major conferences keep telling the same story. To achieve the SDGs, developing countries need to invest in transforming their economies. Historically, no country has achieved developed country status without industrializing, and this premise remains true today. The least developed countries, LDCs, and landlocked developing countries, LLDCs, continue to face challenges in structural transformation and economic diversification, as the reports of the Secretary-General affirm. Over 80% of exports continue to be in primary commodities, making them exceptionally vulnerable to shocks. Agriculture remains a primary employer, but most countries are yet to establish strong linkages between agriculture and the industrial sector. Their economies continue to account for less than 1% of global manufacturing, and manufacturing also remains concentrated in low technology industries. Supporting countries to build productive capacities and local value addition for increased self-sufficiency, economic diversification, and job creation lies at the heart of UNIDO's work. Our 2024 industrial development report emphasizes that every job in manufacturing continues to create on average 2.2 jobs in other sectors of the economy. Developing countries, therefore, need targeted investments in industry, which is also highlighted in the Compromiso de Sevilla. Ladies and gentlemen, UNIDO is committed to supporting LDCs and LLDCs in addressing their unique challenges through concrete industry solutions. Our flagship programs, such as those on agro-industrial parks, contribute to rural industrialization, food system transformation, and job creation. In Ethiopia, for instance, UNIDO is supporting the development of four such parks. To ensure fair participation in global and regional value chains, UNIDO implements programs that specifically target SME competitiveness, for instance, through upskilling in digital technologies and support to national quality control systems. Our interventions align with the global frameworks from the Doha Program of Action for LDCs to the Avaza Program of Action for LDC3, prioritizing structural transformation. Currently, we're working together with the African Union Commission towards a fourth industrial development decade for Africa or IDD4 to support the continent's economic transformation, which also hosts the majority of LDCs and LLDCs. We will continue to host the biennial LDC ministerial conference in coordination with our partners from OHRLLS. The 11th edition, themed Driving Inclusive Industrialization, Investment, Innovation and Partnerships in LDCs, will take place in November 2025 in Saudi Arabia on the margins of the 21st session of our General Conference. UNIDO looks forward to continuing to work with all of you through concrete solutions on the ground. Please count on our full support. Thank you very much.
